cl_nic_smoking_health.q: How much does smoking cigarettes shorten life?
cl_nic_smoking_health.short: About 11 to 12 years on average, a big US study estimates. That's the gap between people who smoked cigarettes and people who never did.
cl_nic_smoking_health.but: These are group averages from one US study. They're not a forecast for any one person.
how: Before age 80, people who smoked died at about 3 times the rate of people who never smoked. For lung cancer, about 15 to 18 times.
Of 100 women aged 25 who smoked, 38 would live to 80, against 70 of 100 who never smoked. For men: 26 against 61.
People who stopped gained years over those who kept smoking: roughly 10 when they stopped at 25 to 34, and 4 at 55 to 64.
A 2014 US Surgeon General's report also judges that smoking raises the risk of dying. It says smoking causes disease in nearly every organ.
cl_nic_smoking_health.rate: One large nationwide study, linked to death records. It didn't account for diet, exercise or income, but those are unlikely to explain a death rate three times as high. The figures on stopping are rougher.

cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.q: Is it the nicotine or the smoke that does the harm?
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.short: Burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm, a big US report says. But it judges that nicotine alone can still harm an unborn baby.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.but: It doesn't say how much of smoking's harm comes from nicotine itself.
how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report looked at both. It says burned tobacco, like cigarettes, causes by far most of tobacco's death and disease in the US.
Nicotine alone can poison at high enough amounts, the report found. It also judged that nicotine harms an unborn baby's brain and adds to early births and stillbirths.
The brain finding comes from lab studies. The pregnancy one comes mostly from smokeless tobacco and nicotine patch trials.
On cancer, the evidence was too thin to say either way. The report calls it likely that nicotine adds somewhat to heart risk in people who smoke.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.rate: One big US government report that sums up other studies and doesn't say how it found them. For nicotine on its own, it leans mostly on animal studies and other products, with few studies of people using nicotine alone.

cl_nic_smoke_nearby.q: Is secondhand tobacco smoke really harmful?
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.short: Yes, two big US reports judge. Others' tobacco smoke is linked to sudden infant death, and to lung cancer and heart disease in adults who don't smoke.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.but: These are the reports' judgments of other studies, so the figures are second-hand. And the later report builds on the earlier.
how: The 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence that others' smoke causes sudden infant death. It found the same for children's chest and ear illness, and asthma at school age.
In adults who don't smoke, living with someone who smokes went with a 20 to 30% higher lung cancer risk. Heart disease and stroke risks were raised about as much.
The 2006 report says no level of secondhand smoke is risk-free. By our reading, that rests mostly on lab findings. Cancer risk is lower than from smoking, it says.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.rate: Two US government reports that sum up other studies, and the later builds on the earlier. We saw only their summaries, which is why the evidence counts as very limited here, not because the reports doubted the links.

cl_nic_cigars.short: It seems so. In big US studies, people who smoked only cigars died of mouth cancer 4 to 8 times as often as people who never smoked.
cl_nic_cigars.but: The studies began decades ago, mostly with white men who smoked big cigars. And the review of them didn't compare cigars with cigarettes.
how: Deaths from voice-box cancer were about 10 times as common, and from lung cancer 2 to 5 times. Deaths from any cause were only slightly higher.
Risks mostly rose with more cigars a day and with inhaling the smoke.
In one big old study, even people who said they didn't inhale died more often of mouth, gullet and voice-box cancer. A newer one had too few to be sure.
cl_nic_cigars.rate: The links are big and grew with more cigars, which helps. But the studies are old, mostly of white men, took little but age into account, and come through one review that didn't judge their quality.

cl_nic_snus.short: It may be. Among Swedish men who never smoked, those who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco.
cl_nic_snus.but: This can't show snus caused it: men who used snus also drank more. And no source we read compared their death rate with people who smoke.
how: Snus is a moist tobacco from Sweden that isn't smoked. In the biggest study, the gap grew with the years men had used it.
An independent review estimated gullet cancer at about 55 in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 who used no tobacco. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference.
A review paid for by a snus maker found no clear harm. A world cancer agency rates smokeless tobacco as causing cancer, without rating snus on its own.
cl_nic_snus.rate: Studies of Swedish men, most from one group of construction workers, with snus use asked once. Men who used snus also drank more, and the sources disagree; one of them was paid for by a snus maker.

cl_nic_pouches.short: Nobody knows yet. No study has followed people who use nicotine pouches for more than 6 months, or looked at disease or death.
cl_nic_pouches.but: Most of what's known comes from lab tests and surveys, not from people's health. And the products differ a lot.
how: Nicotine pouches hold nicotine but no tobacco. A German government lab found nicotine in 44 products bought online in 2021, in very different amounts. Only 15 printed it in milligrams.
Traces of nitrosamines, cancer-causing chemicals from tobacco, turned up in 26 of the 44. Levels were far below those reported for snus.
A review describes one small German study. In it, the two strongest pouches tested raised blood pressure and stiffened arteries about as much as a cigarette.
That review's authors say pouches may be less harmful than tobacco. They add that pouches aren't risk-free.
cl_nic_pouches.rate: Mostly lab tests of products and surveys of who uses them, not studies of health. The studies in people were small and short, and several were paid for by pouch or tobacco makers.

cl_nic_nrt_forms.q: Nicotine patch, gum or both: which works best for quitting smoking?
cl_nic_nrt_forms.short: A nicotine patch plus nicotine gum or similar did a little better than one alone. About 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more, against 14.
cl_nic_nrt_forms.but: Most people in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day. So they say little about lighter smoking.
how: Nicotine replacement means products like nicotine patches, gum, lozenges, inhalers and nose sprays. A patch plus a quick form, like gum, did better than either one alone.
A quick form alone against the patch alone showed no clear difference: about 15 in 100 quit, against 16. That doesn't rule out the patch doing somewhat better.
By our count, over half the trials had links to the products' makers. The review didn't check this, judging it mattered less when comparing ways to use them.
cl_nic_nrt_forms.rate: Strong: 16 trials comparing ways of using these products, with results that agree. One catch: over half had links to the products' makers, which the review didn't weigh.

cl_nic_nrt_harms.q: What side effects do nicotine patches and gum have?
cl_nic_nrt_harms.short: Irritation where they're used: the skin for nicotine patches, the mouth for nicotine gum. Chest pain or a pounding heart: 2.5 in 100, against 1.4 without.
cl_nic_nrt_harms.but: These come from trials lasting weeks to months. Serious problems were too rare to compare.
how: Patches can irritate the skin, usually mildly: up to 54 in 100 people in one source a review cites. Gum can bring hiccups, stomach upset, jaw pain and mouth problems.
Chest pain or a pounding heart was counted in only 15 trials. A patch trial in people with heart disease didn't find more serious problems with the patch.
Side effects made more people stop a quick form, like gum or a nose spray, than the patch: about 23 against 5 in 1,000. That's very uncertain.
cl_nic_nrt_harms.rate: Trials where chance decided who got nicotine, but they recorded side effects differently, and only 15 of 136 counted chest pain or a pounding heart, with fairly few cases. Serious problems were too rare to judge.

cl_nic_vapes_stopping.q: Do nicotine vapes work better than patches or gum for quitting smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.short: Yes, somewhat. In trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a nicotine vape than with nicotine patches or gum.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.but: In most trials that checked, more people kept using the vape than kept using patches or gum. And effects over years aren't known.
how: If 6 in 100 quit with nicotine patches or gum, as a Cochrane review assumes, about 10 in 100 would quit with a nicotine vape.
All trials were in adults, most handed out the vape, and the result held without the one trial paid for by industry.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.rate: Many trials where chance decided who got a vape. The review rates the evidence strong, but we rate it moderate: results varied between trials, and some small trials that found nothing may be unpublished.

cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.q: Do nicotine vapes actually help people quit smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.short: It may help. In trials, about 4 more in 100 quit for 6 months or more when given a nicotine vape than with counselling alone or nothing.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.but: People knew they got a vape, and the vape groups got more support too. So part of the gap may come from the extra help.
how: A Cochrane review assumes 5 in 100 would quit with counselling alone or nothing. Given a nicotine vape, about 9 in 100 would.
All trials were in adults, and longer effects are unknown. The result held without the one trial paid for by a vape company.
Just advising people to vape, without giving them one, made no clear difference.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.rate: Eleven trials where chance decided who got a vape, with results that agree. But people knew what they got, and the vape groups had more support, so the true gain may be smaller.
